items.title: Hollywood Star Charles Esten Gets REAL About Jesus and Faith
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "Blessed."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Actor Charles Esten has had a long, successful career in Hollywood. And while he often opens up about that experience, it’s his faith that has set the roots of truth and goodness in his life, with the performer sharing that his family took him to church early on.

“From an early age, it was part of my family’s week … going to church,” he said. “That was always part of it, and I had wonderful pastors growing up, and great youth involvement.”

Esten, star of the new film “Drummer Boy” — a movie in which he plays a Revolutionary War-era British Lord — said everyone needs to, at some point, make their own profession of faith.

“In Disneyland, they have those big gates where the whole family can go in if you’ve got two strollers and … the whole family walks in,” he said. “That’s not how a relationship… and faith works. It’s more the individual turnstile —you’ve got to find your way to that connection.”

Esten credited his parents with giving him spiritual guidance that helped him grow and learn from their examples.

“I was blessed by a mother that showed me the way and brought me to church and is such a good, loving person and lives out her faith very well,” he said. “And a father that … openly shared with me how he did it wrong. He taught me to be a better man, a better father, a better Christian.”

Esten said his dad’s efforts to focus on what not to do helped him navigate his own faith, with humility driving much of that journey.

“He was very open with that,” he said. “And it was a good blessing to me in my walk.”

Esten also spoke about the balance between “heart and mind” and apologetics. But he warned that even with good apologetics, a person must also radiate God’s love and spirit in order to reach others.

“You always have to have the balance of the heart and the mind … and just somebody that can just do their apologetics right down the line but isn’t radiating any kind of love or any of God’s spirit — that’s a problem too,” he said. “I always felt in and around the love, and the warmth, and the spirit of it all, the mind of it all, was another proof of it to me.”

As for “Drummer Boy,” Esten said the film has something for everyone.

“It’s about faith and family,” he said of the movie. “This movie’s for everyone.”

The actor spoke about his penchant for stories that deal with grace and truth, noting that it’s sometimes most pertinent to tell a story about these subjects through an antagonist — or a person who’s struggling to live them out.

“One of the ways to, I think, illustrate the power of grace is to show characters that are rejecting it, and to show characters that don’t have any,” Esten said. “Sometimes, maybe that can be difficult because that makes for a harder-going movie that’s less family-friendly.”

items.title: Tech Chaos and the End Times: Christian Veteran Warns Against Hyperdependence on AI
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "I began to notice a massive shift..."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Amid a surge of tech outages sweeping industries across the U.S., combat veteran and author Ben Peterson is sounding the alarm that Americans are becoming too dependent on technologies — and not just for gathering information. Many, he warned, are using quickly evolving AI tools to outsource thinking, decision-making, and even relational navigation.

He told CBN News he is witnessing an alarming trend among young military personnel, who are using technology to process conversations and make personal decisions for them.

“I began to notice a massive shift — at least in the last two years, especially in our Gen Z population — of young people that are joining the military, and they’re beginning to rely on artificial intelligence to think for them,” he said. “Before they respond to something, they put it into the chat and say, ‘Hey, how should I handle this? You know me better than I know myself. I trust you more than I trust myself. Help me and think for me.'”

Peterson, who was deployed to Iraq from 2008 to 2009, where he served as a chaplain’s assistant, described a growing dependency on chatbots for guidance and direction, noting he’s seen the next generation eschewing the use of their own judgment on issues.

The data bears out what he’s saying, too. Over the summer, the Barna Group released data showing more than half (62%) of “practicing Christians” described trusting AI’s advice for their “mental and physical wellbeing” and nearly half (48%) said they’d trust the technology’s guidance for their spiritual growth. Additionally, 30% of American adults said advice from AI “is just as trustworthy as advice from a pastor.”

But even to the people who make a concerted effort to avoid artificial intelligence, there is only so much they can do. The technology, he said, is becoming increasingly ubiquitous. Peterson noted, for example, it has been integrated into social media, search engines, banking, the medical industry, and many other everyday services.

“We can run,” he said, “but we can’t hide.”

While the spate of outages and disruptions have been concerning to many, Peterson urged Christians not to respond with fear or become consumed by speculation about the end times — a hot topic when it comes to AI and other nascent technologies. Instead, he emphasized living faithfully, investing in future generations and maintaining a daily relationship with God.

Believers, he emphasized, should be opening their Bibles before picking up their phones to scroll social media or pore over the news. Peterson also urged Christians to balance their study of the end times with living in the here-and-now and investing in what is going on in the world.

“If I live with a scarcity and an end times — constant end times mindset — I think it puts us in a place of consistent fear and, [can prompt us to think things like,] ‘Well, what’s this for anyways?'” he said, noting he’s living in the “tension” of not hyper-fixating on identifying possible signs of the end times while at the same time “being prepared for the imminent return of Christ.”

However, Peterson didn’t mince words about the role he believes AI will play in the end times. He said, “Do I think that AI is setting us up for absolute world disaster and for the end times? Without question.”

“This is going to start moving so fast — and I think we’re starting to experience these birth pains,” Peterson added, referring to Matthew 24:8, where Jesus described to His followers the end-times signs that will precede His second coming.

But perspective is important. When so many things — like artificial intelligence — are vying for our constant attention and often spark anxieties, Peterson said believers ought to look for opportunities to pursue God in their day-to-day lives, by serving others, dedicating time for prayer and Scripture reading, and learning how to be sensitive to the Holy Spirit.

“Everyone wants to make this massive impact on the world and to feel like they’re in the middle of God’s will and accomplishing everything that they want to do with their destiny and with their life, but how often do we overlook the little things?” he asked, adding, “Jesus said he who’s faithful with little is given much.”

And rather than turning to chatbots for direction and guidance, Peterson urged people to turn to God in prayer. In James 1:5, it says, “If you need wisdom, ask our generous God, and he will give it to you. He will not rebuke you for asking” (NLT).

“He’s going to show up,” Peterson said of the Lord. “If you draw near to Him, He’s going to draw near to you. And He is brilliant. He has all of the solutions for every situation that we’ll ever face and that we’ll ever need.”

When the news is discouraging or even distressing, Peterson suggested turning to gratitude, a “vice grip on fear.”

“When you walk in constant gratitude,” he said, “it is like a vice grip on fear, on pride, on all those things, because you just live in a place of humility.”

items.title: RAYE Just Got the Most Grammy Nominations of Anyone, for an Album Full of Faith
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: RAYE is the most-nominated artist at the 2027 Grammys. The British singer picked up 11 nominations this week, including Album of the Year for This Music May Contain Hope and both Record and Song of the Year for “Where Is My Husband!” Rosalía is next with nine. Both made albums steeped in their faith
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

RAYE is the most-nominated artist at the 2027 Grammys. The British singer picked up 11 nominations this week, including Album of the Year for This Music May Contain Hope and both Record and Song of the Year for “Where Is My Husband!” Rosalía is next with nine. Both made albums steeped in their faith in God.

The haul ties Beyoncé’s record for the most nominations by a woman in a single year, according to the Associated Press, and it puts RAYE in three of the four biggest categories for the first time. She has never won a competitive Grammy. The ceremony is Feb. 7 in Los Angeles.

She found out surrounded by family and posted the video to Instagram with a caption that was mostly capital letters and crying emoji: “WHAT IS HAPPENING WHAT IS HAPPENING.”

The album behind all those nominations has God all over it.

RAYE grew up in church in Croydon, south London, where her dad led the music and her mom sang in the choir. She drifted, struggled and got sober, and she’s been plain about what brought her back.

“There’s a world in which if I didn’t find faith again, I might not even be here,” she told the BBC. “There’s a lot of demons trying to claw at you and drag you to somewhere you don’t belong, so I’m really grateful I have this faith. It’s honestly pulled me out of a really dark place.”

That story runs all through This Music May Contain Hope. “Joy,” which she made with her sisters Amma and Absolutely, is a full-throated gospel song, and it borrows from the Psalms to get there. The chorus is Psalm 30:5: “I may cry through the night / But my joy comes in the morning.” Another line is a prayer straight out of Psalm 91: “Cover me with Your feathers, Father / Shelter me with Your wings.”

“Life Boat,” one of her 11 nominated songs, includes the line “Lord, send me a lifeboat.” Gospel choir Flames Collective sings on the record, and when she performed “Joy” on The Late Show this spring, she brought a choir with her.

She told The Times earlier this year where she goes when she’s looking for something to hold onto: “I look for answers in a Bible app, not cruising Instagram.”

Rosalía’s album is up against RAYE’s for Album of the Year. Lux is steeped in Catholic mysticism: It’s sung in 13 languages, with fragments of Latin, Arabic and Hebrew, the cover shows Rosalía in a white nun’s veil, and the songs include “Dios es un stalker” (“God Is a Stalker”) and “Mio Cristo Piange Diamanti” (“My Christ Weeps Diamonds”). She read the lives of female saints from around the world while making it.

“I pray every night before I fall asleep,” Rosalía told The Guardian. “It’s a very personal relationship with God.” She told NPR her grandmother “was the one who put me into God.”

The Grammys are Feb. 7. “Joy,” as RAYE sings it, comes in the morning.

items.title: Tyson Fury is Rebranding the God‑Fearing Family Man
items.author: Johanna Duncan
items.summary:
Johanna Duncan

The show is a refreshing and unexpected testament to the value of a father—even when this one is flawed and struggling with mental illness.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Johanna Duncan

A marital fight is raging as Tyson stops, looks at the camera crew, and asks, “Does anyone know the definition of a narcissist?”

“I found it,” his wife Paris says and proceeds to read, “The definition of a narcissist is ‘a UK-born boxer called Tyson Fury.’”

Momentarily, they are giggling. That scene does plenty to introduce the audience to what it is like to be married to a man who fills Madison Square Garden and has the power to have the whole arena scream his name. It perfectly encapsulates most of what Netflix’s hit show At Home with the Furys is about. The plot follows the world’s heavyweight champion and third highest paid athlete as he faces his retirement—or it may be more appropriate to say his refusal to retire. The cast encompasses his wife Paris Fury, who has been with him since they were teenagers and married in a Catholic ceremony when she was nineteen and he was twenty, their seven children, and Tyson’s dad, John Fury. John is the proud patriarch of the Fury boxing dynasty as a former professional boxer himself and the father of five sons, three of which are professional boxers. Tyson, named after Mike Tyson, is the most successful of them all. 

The reality show is sold to the audience as an inside look into Tyson Fury’s retirement, but the real plot that has taken the audience fully captive revolves around this six-foot-nine giant answering some of the most important questions about life: 

What is one to do after achieving everything one ever wanted before even turning forty? 

What is the purpose of life when material and earthly success loses its meaning? 

What is life about?

Inevitably, the answers to these questions dig deep into Tyson’s relationship with God and love for his family, and, consequently, the show has become an unexpected apostolate for the God-fearing man and the family man—titles Tyson holds with pride. 

While most reality TV is filled with dating shows revolving around petty drama and sleeping around, and the image of fatherhood in widely popular shows such as The Simpsons and Family Guy is degraded to someone who is foolish and lost, At Home with the Furys is a refreshing and unexpected testament to the value of a father—even when this one is flawed and struggling with mental illness. 

Tyson’s mental health plays a pivotal role in the show. He openly discusses his struggles with bipolar disorder, crippling depression, alcoholism, and even drug abuse at one point. He does not shy away from revealing the dark places these have taken him. During his Joe Rogan interview a few years ago, Tyson goes into further detail and discusses a suicide attempt in which he claims to have heard God’s voice urging him to think about what it would do to his wife and children. He chose to live that fateful night, and in the show, we see what he chose to live for. 

In the interview, he shares that after the suicide attempt, his own father took him to see a psychiatrist for the first time and in private. The doctor told John Fury that Tyson’s faith was the only thing keeping him alive at that point, but he warned that his faith could crumble and therefore, he could not be left alone. John Fury recognized what a painful task this was for Paris, who was pregnant and caring for their four young children at the time, so John moved into their home in order to care and keep an eye on his struggling son. 

Tyson and his family never pretend that faith and grace erase suffering. The struggles are taken on with the same openness and willingness as the successes. The real lesson is how to not become reduced to our suffering or successes. In an interview about the show, Paris addresses the matter and shares that she truly believes in until death do us part and in sickness and in health, so leaving Tyson was never a consideration for her in the midst of their painful experiences. 

During the show, this dark period is often referenced, and there is a constant fear that Tyson’s retirement could throw him back into that dark place once again. But I can tell you as a spoiler, it doesn’t. While the mental health struggles persist, Tyson navigates them by embracing his role as husband and father, which proves to be enough to keep him going. 

The questions regarding Tyson’s purpose in life takes the viewer on a journey similar to that of George Bailey in It’s a Wonderful Life. Just like George, Tyson has a clear picture of what the world would be without him in it, and this awareness drives him forward. The show includes family fights and joys alike, and the domestic footage on Netflix becomes a sort of advertisement for the kind of God-fearing family man TV screens have long forgotten about. 

I didn’t know much about Tyson Fury before watching the show, and what I’ve learned about his past (though somewhat current) struggles enriches the story with the extent a man will go for his family. This proves to be even more than what he’d do for himself.

That is the charm of Tyson Fury. 

After watching a few episodes, it becomes clear that Tyson is not really looking for a purpose. He already has that. What he needs is a job, since he’s certainly too young and restless for a life of full-time golfing and fishing. There is an occasional mention of how in other sports, players have a team or community to support them, but boxers navigate their careers mostly alone. It’s a painful trap in which it seems like there’s no life or identity outside this specific high achievement. While Tyson does struggle with this, it’s also evident how his responsibilities as a father pull him out of it.

Order Your Set Today

As part of the Irish Traveller community the Furys belong to, it is common for children to leave school and become apprentices of their parents. This is another permanent plot in the show. At one point, he takes his oldest daughter out for dinner, and they discuss what she’d like to do in the future both professionally and in regards to marriage. 

Then, there are boxing training scenes that involve multiple generations of the Fury dynasty preparing for fights. The pride his sons take in being able to train with their father, grandfather, and uncles is quite evident. It is even more touching when his thirteen-year-old son comes up to him and asks for his father’s blessing to start fighting professionally. Tyson says no and explains that given the fact that he’s not an average fighter but one who belongs to a legendary dynasty, he needs further training before competing. His son respects and accepts his father’s wisdom. 

But my favorite scene in regards to Tyson’s fatherhood comes later when he does a school pickup and excitedly receives his children’s report cards. He cannot wait to get home, so he reads them aloud on the drive home from school. One of his son’s report cards (ironically the one named after him, Tyson) suggests that the young boy could have inherited similar mental health issues to his father. Tyson is visibly touched by this and responds by saying, “My next big fight might be at home.” This is one of the special and ever-present moments in the show that reminds both Tyson and the viewing audience of the value of a present father. It also paints a picture of how regardless of all the success this giant, multimillionaire, undefeated boxer may enjoy, he acknowledges that there are things only a father can do for his children. 

In his 2020 apostolic letter on St. Joseph, Patris Corde, Pope Francis describes fatherhood not as perfection but presence—a man who takes responsibility for others and gives himself to them. Tyson is an example of that to the men searching who may not even be aware of what is missing. And while he already had a platform, the Netflix show has provided a more intimate and deeper look into the message Tyson has been preaching. The show never intends to show the Furys as perfect people, and their imperfections are evident, but the narratives never lose the main plot: Tyson’s triumph. Not the boxing triumph, but his biggest triumph: showing up for his wife and children in spite of every mental health diagnosis. 

What At Home with the Furys has to offer viewers who have grown cynical about marriage and happy-ever-afters is an opportunity to watch two people, flawed and devoted, choose each other—over and over, on camera, for two seasons running and a third currently in production. 

Tyson and Paris never look at the camera to explain themselves or their decisions; instead, the footage of their domestic bliss and torments says it all. They make the case for a fruitful marriage without a pulpit or a script but by simply living in accordance with it. Netflix points a camera crew at one household trying to live their vocations, with imperfections and all, and that is more than enough. But to me and likely to many others, the Furys’ story is enriched by the fact that it was close to not happening. It was close to ending tragically and sooner. Due to the devotion of a man to his family and his strength to fight for them, we now see Tyson still standing as a God-fearing family man defending his titles. 

Somewhere between the retirement plans and children screaming, a show about a legendary fighter leaving the ring became a picture of what faith can produce. It is a story of love, strength, and redemption found in the place where many have forgotten to look: family. 

Maybe I was biased watching the show; maybe this is all truly just about boxing, money, and fame. But for the skeptics, Tyson recently pinned a video to his Instagram addressing a common critique he gets: Why all the praise to God when it is you who trains, prepares, and throws the punches? 

He captioned the video “Setting the record straight for all to hear,” and said,

Nothing that I have is of my doing alone. A man has nothing without God. You can have all the riches in the world and all the material assets, but without God, it means nothing. I’ve been blessed truly and abundantly billions and billions of times. With money, achievements, glory, great career, but most of all, my Savior has given me my soulmate, my wife Paris. And he’s said, “What God has put together no man can tear apart,” and beyond that, blessed us unbelievably with beautiful healthy children. The rest is not important. The belts, boxing fights, all that is just icing on the cake. To be a happy, healthy, and out of trouble man, and a family man is everything that I ever aspired to be. And to be the heavy champion of the world and do as well as I’ve done is icing on that cake, and all glory must go to God. God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—without that, I am nothing. I am just a bare bum in the shower, I am a mortal sinner, and for his grace alone I am saved.

Perhaps the Fury boxing dynasty and Tyson’s personal legacy is about a lot more than just boxing.

items.title: A Guide to the Proverbial Life
items.author: Henry T. Edmondson III
items.summary:
Henry T. Edmondson III

In a time in which we must run to keep up with technology and change, the Book of Proverbs offers ancient, unhurried wisdom.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Henry T. Edmondson III

The best way to read the Book of Proverbs is to read one proverb at a time, followed by a moment of reflection, if not more extended meditation. Unlike other passages of the Bible, most of the proverbs stand alone and are not dependent on the passages that come before and after to complete their meaning. But meaningful meditation might mean getting no farther than four or five verses, if that far—an experience reminiscent of what Jeremiah said, “Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart; for I am called by your name” (Jer 15:16).

Taken this way, the proverbs can filter down into the soul, becoming part of a receptive, reflective heart. The proverbs themselves observe, “Desire without knowledge is not good, and one who moves too hurriedly misses the way” (Prov 19:2). 

Notably, the Church has long recognized a special relationship between the wisdom of Proverbs and the role of Mary in the Church. The Catechism of the Catholic Church explains that “as the Father found the dwelling place where the Son and the Spirit could dwell among men,” so “the Church’s Tradition has often read the most beautiful texts on wisdom,” such as in the Book of Proverbs, “in relation to Mary.” Indeed, in the very first chapter, wisdom is personified as a woman: “Wisdom cries out in the street; in the squares she raises her voice” (Prov 1:20). 

The Book of Proverbs is concerned with living rightly. The proverbs are practical—at times, even gritty. For example, once started, an argument it is hard to stop: “The beginning of strife is like letting out water; so stop before the quarrel breaks out” (Prov 17:14).

At the same time, the proverbs are written with a view toward eternity. This attitude is often expressed by the phrase “the fear of the Lord,” which is so conspicuous in Proverbs. 

The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction (1:7). 

Although duty and honor are important in Proverbs, these ideals are not the first motivation of right conduct for the Christian; rather, piety before God is paramount. 

Wisdom and Folly

According to Proverbs, both the foundation and goal of an upright life is wisdom. The proverbs, however, are concerned with more than human wisdom—they are an invitation to share in the wisdom of God himself. When, in chapter 3, the proverb says to “get wisdom,” it also explains, “The Lord by wisdom founded the earth; by understanding he established the heavens” (3:19).

The proverbs also suggest that one of the rewards of the wise and virtuous is peace. Proverbs 14:30 explains, “A tranquil mind gives life to the flesh.”

This is an answer to the question that perplexes the psalmist when he asks why the wicked may prosper and the righteous may not. In Psalm 73:3, David admits, “I was envious of the arrogant; I saw the prosperity of the wicked.” If righteous people do not always see material rewards for their faithfulness, however, they can at least count on the things that money can’t buy: a good conscience, peace of mind, and membership in the Church.

St. Augustine underscores the importance of Proverbs’ wisdom, quoting Proverbs 9:1, “Wisdom has built her house, she has hewn her seven pillars.” For Augustine, the “house” prefigures the Church of Christ, and the number seven represents the perfection and divinity that only God’s wisdom can supply. To be sure, Augustine’s mentor, St. Ambrose, in his extensive Lenten catechesis for converts to the Church, used “the lives of the patriarchs and the maxims of the Book of Proverbs.”

The opposite of wisdom is folly, personified in chapters 2, 5, 6, and 7 as a “woman of adultery.” The warnings against adultery are not only a warning to men against marital unfaithfulness. They are also a warning to all Christians against the danger of “spiritual adultery”: wandering from our first love—Christ and his Church—toward the temptations of the “world, the flesh, and the devil.” For example, St. John Chrysostom refers to Proverbs 7 as a warning against covetousness in general and the love of money in particular. 

For this is the advice the writer of Proverbs gives us, when he speaks about the harlot: “Spring away,” he says, “tarry not, neither go thou near to the door of her house.” 

Also opposed to wisdom is a prideful disposition: “All those who are arrogant are an abomination to the Lord” (16:5). 

When “pride comes,” moreover, “disgrace” quickly follows. On the other hand, “with humility comes wisdom” (11:2 NIV). Unless a person cultivates humility by admitting the need for wisdom and displays a willingness to accept correction, wisdom will remain out of reach. Humility means a willingness to receive correction.

A rebuke strikes deeper into a discerning person than a hundred blows into a fool (17:10).

These days, it sometimes seems that hardly anyone aspires to be “wise.” Many seek to be “successful,” “happy,” “cool”—or they do not aspire to be anything, rather just to do or to have or to experience. Ultimately, of course, wisdom comes from God, and as smart as we may think we are, our meager wits are trumped by God’s wisdom countless times over.

Trust in the Lord with all your heart, 
and do not rely on your own insight. 
In all your ways acknowledge him, 
and he will make straight your paths (3:5–6).

Notably, this Proverb was the favorite Scripture of Vice President Gerald Ford. When he swore his oath to enter office after Nixon’s resignation, he had his Bible open to this same passage.

The Enlivening Power of Speech and the Destructiveness of Mockery

Among the conspicuous themes in the Book of Proverbs is the power that speech has for good or for evil. The proverbs reveal that “death and life are in the power of the tongue” (18:21).

“Kind words” can make all the difference in our neighbor’s well-being. One of the more beautiful proverbs describing the power of speech reads, “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver” (25:11). Abraham Lincoln found this passage so attractive that he used it as the theme of one of his speeches, in which he argued that the principles of the Declaration of Independence are the “apples of gold” that are “framed” by the “setting of silver”—the US Constitution. 

On the other hand, words have the capacity to discourage and annoy. One proverb even warns against annoying speech before the first cup of coffee, no matter how well-intentioned: “Whoever blesses a neighbor with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, will be counted as cursing” (27:14). 

The proverbs also warn against “mockery.” The condemnation of mockery is as relevant today as it was millennia ago. Sometimes, however, mockery is not recognized for what it is. Political satire is essential in a democracy for the control of politicians and the health of political institutions. Daily conversations and popular entertainment, though, may go beyond all bounds. TV shows, movies, and stand-up comics rake in millions by mocking all things sacred. A frightening revelation of the Book of Proverbs is that the individual who engages in mockery will never be helped—so long as he is a mocker. Prov 9:7 says, “Whoever corrects a mocker invites insults; whoever rebukes the wicked incurs abuse” (NIV).

The mocker must renounce his misbehavior first; judgment against mockery can be brutal. For example, when the prophet Elisha was traveling from Bethel to Mt. Carmel, a group of local delinquents jeered, “Go away, baldhead!” Elisha “turned around and saw them, he cursed them in the name of the Lord. Then two she-bears came out of the woods and mauled forty-two of the boys” (2 Kings 2:23-25).

A Good Name, Prudence, and Justice

The value of a good name can be discounted. This, in turn, suggests a life guided by prudence. Whereas wisdom is a storehouse of knowledge and principles, prudence takes those principles and applies them to daily challenges.

Sometimes prudence seems little more than common sense: “Better to meet a she-bear robbed of its cubs than to confront a fool immersed in folly” (17:12). This implies that there are some people who should be given a wide berth. Just take the next elevator.

Other times, prudence provides guidance through the perplexities and hazards of life: “The clever see danger and hide; but the simple go on, and suffer for it” (27:12). 

As the Catechism observes, “The prudent man looks where he is going.” Prudence guides other virtues, like courage or justice, helping us to know just when and how and where to be courageous or just. Prudence also unravels some of the apparent contradictions in Scripture. For example, in dealing with fools, Proverbs 26:4 advises, “Do not answer fools according to their folly, or you will be a fool yourself.” But the next verse seems to contradict the first: “Answer fools according to their folly, or they will be wise in their own eyes.”

Isn’t this a contradiction? Maybe not. Different circumstances and different people may call for different responses. But the principle remains the same: You are dealing with a fool. It’s just a matter of letting prudence be your guide.

The proverbs are full of warnings. It may seem strange to assert something so self-evident, but Scripture warns that we can’t escape responsibility for our behavior. The proverbs explain this by borrowing a simple yet effective example from the physical law:

Can fire be carried in the bosom
without burning one’s clothes? 
Or can one walk on hot coals 
without scorching the feet? (6:27-8) 

Of course, there are those who refuse to heed a warning. As we have already noted, there is a special category reserved for them: Proverbs calls them “fools,” and the existence of fools is one of the sad realities of life. Unless they can be shaken from their foolishness, they will stubbornly pursue foolish, self-destructive behavior. The proverb graphically explains, “Like a dog that returns to its vomit is a fool who reverts to his folly” (26:11). 

Care for the Poor and Suffering 

Since the Book of Proverbs is about human conduct, it naturally addresses interpersonal relations, emphasizing justice, mercy, and kindness. The sage warns, “A false balance is an abomination to the Lord, but an accurate weight is his delight” (11:1). 

Advice about kindness is as practical as can be imagined. When people are in distress, we should “Let beer be for those who are perishing, wine for those who are in anguish!” (31:6 NIV)

The Lord has a special place in his heart for the poor. Scripture says, “Those who mock the poor insult their Maker; those who are glad at calamity will not go unpunished” (17:5).
Magnificent Humanity
Get Pope Leo’s Encyclical

The persistence of poverty offers many opportunities for kindness, but not in a detached, condescending way. The Bible teaches that the poor are not just separated economically, but socially as well. Proverbs 19:4 notes, “Wealth brings many friends, but the poor are left friendless.”

For that reason, in the beautiful twelfth chapter of Romans on Christian ethics, Scripture reads, “Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly; do not claim to be wiser than you are” (12:14). Often the best opportunities for this may not be in grand acts of charity but the everyday kindness of asking the custodian about his family, remembering the birthday of the security guard’s kid, and maybe attending the cook’s daughter’s high school graduation.

Slow Down to Catch Up

In a time in which we must run to keep up with technology and change, the Book of Proverbs offers ancient, unhurried wisdom. But to hear that wisdom requires taking a deep breath and prayerfully listening. Understanding and incorporating the wisdom of Proverbs into our lives and lifestyle requires a decision to navigate out of the whitewater currents of modern life, sit beside Psalm 23’s “still waters,” and read, meditate, and contemplate. 

Solomon—whose very name is synonymous with wisdom—is the most conspicuous author of the Book of Proverbs. It is said in the book of Kings that he wrote 3,000 proverbs! Fortunately, the Bible whittles them down to about 800. There are other important themes in the Book of Proverbs not addressed in this article. They include, but are not limited to, spiritual combat, how to handle money, and the famous description of a “virtuous woman” in Proverbs 31. The Book of Proverbs is a guide to a proverbial life.
